title: SYSK Selects: Could You Live Without a Refrigerator?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of a January 2012 episode, introduced by Chuck as his pick. The hosts explore whether people can live without a refrigerator ("defridging"), tracing the 2009 New York Times attention to people unplugging fridges as a green trend. They compare refrigerator energy use with other household appliances, discuss which foods can stay out of the fridge (butter, condiments, onions, tomatoes, potatoes, cilantro, avocados), and cooling alternatives like coolers and chest freezers. The conversation moves to food waste (developing-world post-harvest losses, US food waste in landfills and methane), zero-waste living (Bea Johnson), upcycled shoes and license-plate siding, and a listener mail segment from a St. Louis police officer about a meth lab found in a Gatorade bottle. The episode closes with a segment on Einstein's no-moving-parts refrigerator and tips for keeping an existing fridge efficient.
rerun_of: Could You Live Without a Refrigerator?

segments.title: Opening banter and green movement
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as his select pick. The hosts banter about eco-friendliness, littering, and whether giving up refrigerators is a green fad.

segments.title: Why people unplug refrigerators
segments.summary: The hosts describe the 2009 New York Times article about people giving up refrigerators as a green practice, and compare it to sterilization as a reversible or irreversible choice.

segments.title: Refrigerator energy use vs. other appliances
segments.summary: They give energy-use figures: a post-2000 fridge uses about 450 kWh a year, less than a clothes dryer, central air, or furnace, and is roughly equivalent to about 800 miles of driving in CO2 terms.

segments.title: Foods that don't need refrigeration
segments.summary: The hosts discuss which foods can stay out of the fridge, including butter, ketchup, mustard, hot sauce, onions, tomatoes, potatoes, cauliflower, and cilantro stored in water, plus tips on cutting onions and ripening avocados with a banana in a paper bag.

segments.title: Coolers and chest freezers as alternatives
segments.summary: Without a fridge, people still need some cooling. Defridgers use coolers, and some use small chest freezers, which still use about 2 kWh a year, with frozen water bottles kept in coolers.

segments.title: Shopping and packaging trade-offs
segments.summary: Buying smaller amounts reduces waste but means more packaging and more driving to the store, which can offset the environmental benefit.

segments.title: Food waste, developing countries, and methane
segments.summary: Post-harvest food grain losses in developing countries are discussed. The EPA says food leftovers are the largest part of the waste stream by weight, and landfill food waste produces methane, which is about 21 times more potent than CO2. The hosts discuss livestock methane and trapping it for energy.

segments.title: Zero waste and reusing food
segments.summary: Bea Johnson's zero-waste family and her five Rs (refuse, reduce, reuse, recycle, rot) are discussed, along with reusing stale bread and wilted lettuce, and eating edible weeds. Also mentioned are shoes made from old tires and license plates used as siding.

segments.title: Poop burger and toilet paper alternatives
segments.summary: The hosts question a viral story about a Japanese scientist making burgers from human feces, which they could not verify. They then discuss the London fatberg of wet wipes and grease and cloth-diaper bidets as green toilet paper alternatives.

segments.title: Einstein refrigerator and fridge efficiency tips
segments.summary: The hosts describe Einstein's no-moving-parts absorption refrigerator, which a researcher in Oxford tried to rebuild. They then give tips for keeping an existing fridge efficient: buy an Energy Star model, clean coils yearly, and limit door opening.

segments.title: Listener mail: meth lab in a Gatorade bottle
segments.summary: A St. Louis police officer writes in about a mobile meth lab found in a Gatorade bottle at a Walmart, and about children found in meth labs. The hosts also mention how to send mystery suggestions.
